title: Lessen & Pacify
rule: These words describe making something bad less severe (mitigate, alleviate, attenuate, abate) or making an angry person less hostile (placate, mollify, appease, propitiate). The GRE pairs them with contrast signals such as 'far from,' 'did little to,' and 'rather than,' and its favorite trap is a 'worsen' word (exacerbate) that fits the intent but not the outcome, or a 'cure' word (eradicate) when the sentence only allows partial relief.
tip: Things get mitigated, alleviated, and allayed; people get placated, mollified, and appeased; and palliate (Latin pallium, 'cloak') only cloaks the symptoms without curing the disease.

words.m: to make less severe, serious, or painful
words.s: Engineers argued that wider levees would mitigate, though never wholly prevent, the damage caused by the river's increasingly frequent floods.

words.m: to relieve or lessen pain, suffering, or a problem
words.s: The new subway line was meant to alleviate congestion downtown, but commuters soon complained that traffic was as snarled as ever.
words.root: Latin levis, 'light': to lighten a burden

words.m: to soothe or satisfy; to make an unpleasant feeling less intense
words.s: No public apology could assuage the grief of families who had lost their homes to a fire the company had been warned about for years.

words.m: to soften the anger or hostility of someone
words.s: Hoping to mollify the furious shareholders, the board announced a special dividend and promised a full review of the chief executive's decisions.

words.m: to calm someone's anger, especially by making concessions
words.s: The mayor's vague promise of 'further study' did little to placate residents who had demanded the toxic landfill be closed immediately.
words.root: Latin placare, 'to calm'; kin to placid

words.m: to pacify by granting demands, often at the cost of principle
words.s: Historians still debate whether the diplomats who tried to appease the dictator in 1938 merely bought time or emboldened further aggression.

words.m: to diminish or put to rest a fear, doubt, or suspicion
words.s: The airline released its full maintenance records in an effort to allay passengers' fears after the second engine failure in a month.

words.m: to ease symptoms without curing; to make an offense seem less serious
words.s: The drug can palliate the patient's pain, but it does nothing to halt the underlying disease, which continues to progress unchecked.
words.root: Latin pallium, 'cloak': covers rather than cures

words.m: to weaken or reduce in force, intensity, or value
words.s: Thick stone walls attenuate the noise of the street so effectively that the monastery's cloister remains almost perfectly silent at midday.

words.m: to become or make less intense or widespread
words.s: Rescue crews were forced to wait on the ridge until the storm began to abate, since helicopters could not fly in such winds.

words.m: to moderate or soften something by adding a counterbalancing element
words.s: She learned to temper her criticism with genuine praise, so that junior colleagues heard her suggestions rather than merely bristling at them.
words.root: Latin temperare, 'to mix in due proportion'

words.m: to win or regain the favor of an offended person or deity
words.s: Ancient farmers offered the first fruits of each harvest to propitiate the gods they believed controlled drought, flood, and blight.

tc.q: Although the new regulations were touted as a cure for the region's chronic air pollution, they in fact did no more than _____ it: emissions fell modestly, but the underlying reliance on coal remained untouched.
tc.why: 'Did no more than' plus 'emissions fell modestly' signals partial lessening: mitigate. Eradicate is the trap set by 'touted as a cure'; the sentence explicitly denies a cure, and exacerbate runs the wrong direction.

tc.q: Management's offer of a token raise, delivered alongside a warning about impending layoffs, did nothing to _____ the striking workers; if anything, it hardened their resolve to stay off the job.
tc.why: 'If anything' signals the opposite of the blank, and the actual result was hardened resolve, so the offer failed to soften their anger: mollify. Galvanize and embolden describe what actually happened, not what the offer failed to do.

tc.q: The physician was candid with the family: the treatment could (i) _____ their father's discomfort in his final weeks, but it could not (ii) _____ the growth of the tumor, which had already spread beyond the reach of surgery.
tc.why: The candor contrasts symptom relief with cure: palliate means to ease without curing, and to arrest (halt) the tumor's growth is what the treatment cannot do. Exacerbate reverses the first blank, and accelerate is absurd as something a doctor regrets being unable to do.

tc.q: Critics who expected the senator to (i) _____ her opponents by softening the bill were surprised: rather than offering concessions, she actually (ii) _____ the measure's most contentious provisions, apparently calculating that conciliation would win her nothing.
tc.why: The expectation is defined by 'softening the bill' and 'conciliation': placating her opponents. What surprised critics was the reverse of a concession, so she expanded the provisions; diluted and abandoned are exactly the concessions she refused to make.

se.q: The ambassador's carefully worded statement was designed to _____ the anxieties of allies who feared the treaty would leave them exposed, without committing the government to any new obligations.
se.why: A statement meant to reassure worried allies must lessen their fears: allay and assuage. Exacerbate and kindle form a synonym pair pointing the wrong way; articulate fits the syntax but not the reassuring purpose.

se.q: Though the editor's comments were initially stinging, she was careful to _____ her objections with acknowledgments of the manuscript's considerable strengths.
se.why: The contrast with 'stinging' and the counterweight of praise call for a word meaning to moderate by mixing in something milder: temper and leaven. Bolster and substantiate pair up but would reinforce rather than soften the objections.

se.q: Rather than confronting the restive nobles directly, the young king sought to _____ them with lavish grants of land and title, hoping that gratitude would outweigh ambition.
se.why: 'Rather than confronting' plus 'lavish grants' and 'gratitude' point to winning favor through concessions: propitiate and placate. Subjugate and rebuke are confrontational, exactly what the king avoided.

se.q: The pandemic's economic toll did not _____ until well into the following year, when supply chains finally recovered and unemployment returned to its earlier level.
se.why: Recovering supply chains and falling unemployment show the toll lessened: abate and subside. Escalate and intensify are a synonym pair pointing the wrong way, and materialize and culminate misstate the timeline.

title: Worsen & Provoke
rule: This cluster covers making a bad situation worse (exacerbate, aggravate, compound, deteriorate) and stirring people to anger or action (foment, incite, instigate, goad, exasperate, rankle). On the GRE these usually appear where a well-intentioned action backfires, flagged by 'served only to,' 'far from easing,' or 'if anything,' and the classic trap is a 'lessen' word like mitigate that matches the intent but not the result.
tip: Exacerbate hides Latin acerbus, 'harsh, bitter' (as in acerbic): to make an already bad thing more bitter; compound means to pile one trouble on top of another.

words.m: to make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse
words.s: Cutting the clinic's hours to save money will only exacerbate the backlog, since patients turned away today will return sicker next month.

words.m: to make a condition or offense more serious; also, to annoy
words.s: Lifting heavy boxes so soon after surgery could aggravate the injury and add months to an already slow recovery.

words.m: to make a problem worse by adding to it
words.s: The firm's initial error was understandable, but executives chose to compound it by shredding documents and denying that anything had gone wrong.
words.root: Latin componere, 'to put together': piling trouble on trouble

words.m: to become progressively worse in quality or condition
words.s: Without regular maintenance, the medieval frescoes will continue to deteriorate as humidity seeps through the chapel's crumbling plaster walls.

words.m: to stir up or instigate trouble, rebellion, or discord
words.s: The regime accused foreign journalists of trying to foment unrest, though the protests had clearly grown from long-standing local grievances over food prices.
words.root: Latin fomentum, 'warm poultice': keeping trouble warm

words.m: to encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior
words.s: The court ruled that the speech, however offensive, did not incite violence, because no listener was urged to take any immediate unlawful action.
words.root: Latin incitare, 'to set in rapid motion'

words.m: to bring about or initiate an action or event, often a harmful one
words.s: Investigators were determined to learn who had chosen to instigate the walkout, since the union's elected leaders insisted they had never authorized it.

words.m: to provoke or urge someone into action by annoying them
words.s: The defense attorney tried to goad the witness into an angry outburst, hoping the jury would doubt his composure and therefore his testimony.
words.root: Old English gad, 'pointed stick for driving cattle'

words.m: to irritate intensely; to infuriate through repeated frustration
words.s: His habit of answering every direct question with a rambling anecdote began to exasperate even the most patient members of the committee.
words.root: Latin asper, 'rough': to roughen one's temper

words.m: to cause persistent, festering resentment or irritation
words.s: Years after the merger, the decision to close the original headquarters continued to rankle longtime employees who had helped build the company.
words.root: Old French rancler, 'to fester' (of a wound)

words.m: to irritate or annoy, especially with minor provocations
words.s: The critic's condescending praise seemed calculated to nettle the young novelist, who had hoped for honest engagement rather than a pat on the head.

words.m: to annoy, frustrate, or worry, especially persistently
words.s: The paradox continued to vex mathematicians for decades, resisting every attempt at a solution until a graduate student reframed the problem entirely.

tc.q: The central bank's decision to print money to pay off the nation's debts did not ease the crisis but served only to _____ it, as soaring inflation wiped out the savings that might have cushioned the downturn.
tc.why: 'Did not ease... but served only to' demands the opposite of easing, and inflation wiping out savings shows the problem got worse: compound. Resolve and forestall describe the relief the sentence denies.

tc.q: Although officials blamed outside agitators for the riot, the inquiry found no evidence that anyone had deliberately set out to _____ the crowd; the violence appeared to have erupted spontaneously after a rumor spread.
tc.why: Blaming 'outside agitators' implies someone deliberately stirred the crowd up: incite. The inquiry denies this by citing spontaneity; disperse and placate run counter to the agitator accusation.

tc.q: The commission's report, which was supposed to (i) _____ the longstanding feud between the two ministries, served only to (ii) _____ it, assigning blame so one-sidedly that the aggrieved ministry refused to attend further meetings.
tc.why: 'Supposed to... served only to' contrasts intent with a worse outcome, and the boycott proves the feud deepened: meant to resolve it, the report exacerbated it. Mitigate would match the intent, not the result, and no commission is 'supposed to' foment a feud.

tc.q: Her opponents' constant needling was plainly calculated to (i) _____ her into an intemperate response, yet the candidate remained so (ii) _____ throughout the debate that the strategy backfired, making them look petty instead.
tc.why: Needling meant to produce an 'intemperate response' is goading; coax implies gentle persuasion. 'Yet' and 'backfired' show she never took the bait: unflappable, whereas irascible would mean the strategy worked.

se.q: Critics charged that the pamphleteer had done more than report on the peasants' discontent; he had actively sought to _____ it, distributing tracts that urged open rebellion against the landlords.
se.why: 'Done more than report' plus tracts urging rebellion means he stirred the discontent up: foment and stoke. Quell and suppress pair up in the opposite direction; chronicle and analyze merely restate the reporting he went beyond.

se.q: Although the senator brushed off the slight in public, aides reported that it continued to _____ him privately for months, surfacing in bitter asides whenever his rival's name came up.
se.why: 'Brushed off... in public' contrasts with private 'bitter asides,' so the slight kept irritating him: rankle and gall. Placate and soothe are a synonym pair in the wrong direction; amuse and intrigue lack the bitterness the asides require.

se.q: The supervisor's insistence on personally approving every minor expense, however trivial, served only to _____ a staff already frustrated by months of delayed projects.
se.why: 'Served only to' and 'already frustrated' signal heightened irritation: exasperate and infuriate. Reassure and appease are a near-synonym pair pointing the wrong way, and motivate ignores the frustration.

se.q: Economists warned that the proposed tariffs, rather than protecting domestic manufacturers, would _____ their difficulties by raising the cost of the imported components on which they depend.
se.why: 'Rather than protecting' plus higher component costs means the tariffs would make matters worse: aggravate and exacerbate. Alleviate and mitigate form a tempting pair that describes the intended, not the predicted, effect.

title: Excess & Abundance
rule: These words describe having more than enough, sometimes neutrally or approvingly (copious, prolific, myriad, profusion) and sometimes disapprovingly, as too much (glut, surfeit, superfluous, exorbitant). The GRE often tests whether an abundance is welcome or excessive, so read the tone: 'only cluttered,' 'drowned out,' 'unnecessary,' or 'bore no relation to' point to glut and surfeit, while the classic trap is a scarcity word (dearth, paucity) placed where a contrast has been reversed.
tip: Plethora and replete share the root ple-, 'to fill' (as in plenty and complete), and surfeit is sur- 'over' + fait 'done': literally overdone.

words.m: an excessive or very large amount of something
words.s: The report offered a plethora of statistics but almost no analysis, leaving readers to wonder what conclusions, if any, the authors had actually drawn.

words.m: an oversupply, especially of a commodity, beyond what the market demands
words.s: A global glut of crude oil drove prices so low that many small drillers could no longer cover the cost of pumping it.
words.root: Old French gloutir, 'to swallow' (as in glutton)

words.m: an excessive amount, often to the point of disgust or satiety
words.s: After a surfeit of superhero sequels, audiences seemed hungry for small, character-driven films that did not depend on spectacle.

words.m: a large, often lavish quantity or abundance of something
words.s: Each spring the abandoned railway embankment erupts in a profusion of wildflowers, poppies and lupines crowding every inch of the once-barren gravel.

words.m: abundant in supply or quantity; plentiful
words.s: A meticulous researcher, she took copious notes at every archive she visited, often filling an entire notebook in a single afternoon.

words.m: producing much fruit, offspring, or work; highly productive
words.s: Though remarkably prolific, publishing nearly a novel a year, the author insisted that most of her drafts ended up in the wastebasket.

words.m: countless or extremely great in number
words.s: The biologist marveled at the myriad species of beetle inhabiting a single rainforest tree, many of them entirely unknown to science.

words.m: abundantly filled or well supplied with something
words.s: The biography is replete with vivid anecdotes, yet it rarely pauses to ask what those episodes reveal about its subject's character.

words.m: widespread, especially of something undesirable; full of
words.s: The provincial bureaucracy was rife with corruption, and few contracts were awarded without a bribe passing quietly under the table.

words.m: unnecessary, especially through being more than enough
words.s: The editor struck every superfluous adjective from the draft, arguing that the story's events were dramatic enough without verbal decoration.

words.m: unreasonably high, especially of a price or demand
words.s: Patients without insurance often face exorbitant bills for routine procedures that cost a fraction as much in neighboring countries.
words.root: Latin ex orbita, 'out of the track'

words.m: to overwhelm with things or people to be dealt with; to flood
words.s: Fans began to inundate the station with complaints within minutes of the announcement that the beloved program had been canceled.

tc.q: Rather than clarifying the issue, the committee's 400-page report merely added to the _____ of conflicting data already available, making it even harder for legislators to identify a sensible course of action.
tc.why: 'Rather than clarifying' and 'even harder' show the report piled more onto an already excessive supply: glut. Dearth contradicts 'added to... already available,' and synthesis or consensus would have clarified the issue.

tc.q: The poet's late style is notably spare: where her early collections were _____ with ornate imagery, the final volume confines itself to a few stark, unadorned lines per page.
tc.why: 'Where' sets up a contrast with the spare, unadorned late style, so the early work was filled with ornate imagery: replete. Bereft, sparing, and unencumbered all describe the late style instead.

tc.q: Although the region's (i) _____ rainfall supports a dense, wildly diverse forest, the soil beneath it is surprisingly poor, because the same downpours (ii) _____ nutrients before plant roots can absorb them.
tc.why: 'Downpours' and a dense forest point to plentiful rain: copious, which scant contradicts. 'Although... surprisingly poor' requires the rain to strip nutrients from the soil, so leach away, not replenish.

tc.q: The startup's founders mistook mere activity for productivity: their team was undeniably (i) _____, issuing new features almost weekly, but so many of those features were (ii) _____, duplicating functions the product already had, that users found the interface bewildering.
tc.why: Issuing features almost weekly makes the team prolific, and 'duplicating functions the product already had' defines superfluous. Indolent contradicts the pace, and indispensable or innovative clash with the bewildered users.

se.q: The new minister soon discovered that inefficiency was _____ in the agency: forms were duplicated across departments, and some routine requests required a dozen signatures.
se.why: The examples (duplicated forms, a dozen signatures) show inefficiency was widespread: rife and rampant. Negligible contradicts the evidence, and latent fails because the problem is plainly visible.

se.q: Far from suffering from a shortage of qualified applicants, the program faced a _____ of them, and admissions officers struggled to choose among hundreds of equally impressive candidates.
se.why: 'Far from... a shortage' and 'hundreds of... candidates' call for an overabundance: plethora and surfeit. Paucity and dearth are a synonym pair restating the very shortage the sentence rejects.

se.q: Many longtime tenants were forced out of the neighborhood after landlords began demanding _____ rents that bore no relation to the buildings' dilapidated condition.
se.why: Tenants driven out by rents unrelated to the buildings' poor condition implies unreasonably high rents: exorbitant and extortionate. Nominal and modest form a pair pointing the wrong way, and fluctuating does not explain the exodus.

se.q: Organizers warned that the free concert could _____ the small town's roads and hospitals, which were designed to serve a few thousand residents rather than a hundred thousand visitors.
se.why: 'Warned' and the mismatch between a few thousand residents and a hundred thousand visitors point to being swamped: inundate and overwhelm. Enrich and revitalize are a positive pair that clash with 'warned.'

title: Scarcity & Poverty
rule: These words describe insufficiency, either of things in general (dearth, paucity, scant, meager, sparse, exiguous) or of money in particular (penury, indigent, destitute, impecunious). The GRE often hides them behind contrasts such as 'for all the hype' or 'although the holdings are vast,' and a favorite trap is the stinginess cluster: an impecunious person lacks money, while a parsimonious or miserly one merely refuses to spend it.
tip: Latin pecunia, 'money' (from pecus, 'cattle,' an early form of wealth), makes im-pecunious 'moneyless'; and a dearth is the condition in which things are 'dear' because they are scarce.

words.m: a scarcity or lack of something
words.s: The dearth of reliable records from the period means that historians must reconstruct the village's economy largely from tax rolls and church registers.
words.root: Middle English derthe, 'dearness': scarce things are costly

words.m: the presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities
words.s: Given the paucity of evidence linking the suspect to the crime, prosecutors reluctantly dropped the charges rather than risk an acquittal.

words.m: barely sufficient or less than sufficient in amount
words.s: The proposal received scant attention from the board, which spent nearly the entire meeting debating the color of the new company logo.

words.m: lacking in quantity or quality; deficient
words.s: Despite years of fieldwork, the expedition's meager findings consisted of a few pottery shards and a single, badly corroded bronze coin.

words.m: thinly dispersed or scattered; not dense
words.s: Vegetation grows sparse above the tree line, where only lichens and a few hardy grasses can survive the wind and the brief summer.

words.m: very small in size or amount; scanty
words.s: Researchers working with such exiguous funding could afford only a handful of samples, far too few to support confident conclusions.

words.m: extreme poverty; destitution
words.s: The once-celebrated painter spent his final years in penury, selling sketches for the price of a meal in a rented attic.

words.m: poor; lacking the necessities of life
words.s: Under the new law, the state must provide a lawyer to any indigent defendant who cannot afford to hire one for a felony trial.

words.m: without the basic necessities of life; completely impoverished
words.s: The famine left thousands of families destitute, forced to sell their livestock and seed grain simply to survive until the next harvest.

words.m: having little or no money
words.s: An impecunious graduate student, he survived on instant noodles and borrowed textbooks while writing the dissertation that later made him famous.

words.m: to make poor; to exhaust the strength or richness of
words.s: Decades of planting the same crop year after year can impoverish the soil, stripping it of the nutrients later harvests will need.

words.m: to use up or greatly reduce the supply of something
words.s: Overfishing threatens to deplete the cod stocks so severely that the population may never recover, even if all fishing stops.

tc.q: For all the hype surrounding the new treatment, the _____ of controlled clinical trials means that its effectiveness remains, at best, an open question.
tc.why: 'For all the hype' signals that the evidence falls short, and an open question results from too few trials: dearth. Proliferation, rigor, and success would settle the question rather than leave it open.

tc.q: Although the archive's holdings on the colonial period are vast, its materials on the decades immediately following independence are so _____ that scholars of that era must rely chiefly on oral histories.
tc.why: 'Although... vast' sets up a contrast, and having to 'rely chiefly on oral histories' shows the materials are scanty: exiguous. Exhaustive and authoritative would make oral histories unnecessary.

tc.q: The novelist's portrait of rural life during the Depression avoids sentimentality: her characters are not ennobled by their (i) _____ but rather diminished by it, their generosity and hope gradually (ii) _____ by years of scraping together barely enough to eat.
tc.why: 'Scraping together barely enough to eat' defines the characters' condition as penury, which 'diminished' them, so their generosity and hope were eroded. Affluence contradicts the scarcity, and kindled reverses 'diminished.'

tc.q: Biographers long assumed the composer was (i) _____ in his last decade, but newly discovered bank records show he was in fact quite comfortable; his notoriously (ii) _____ habits, from patched coats to unheated rooms, reflected miserliness rather than need.
tc.why: Bank records showing he was 'quite comfortable' refute the assumption, so biographers thought him destitute; bank records could not refute 'reclusive.' Patched coats and unheated rooms are spartan habits, which reflected miserliness, not poverty: the classic poverty-versus-stinginess distinction.

se.q: The village's water supply, never abundant, had become so _____ by late August that residents were limited to a single bucket per household each day.
se.why: 'Never abundant' and a one-bucket ration show the supply was barely sufficient: meager and scant. Plentiful and ample are a synonym pair that contradict the ration.

se.q: Because the clinic served a largely _____ population, it charged fees on a sliding scale, and many of its patients paid nothing at all.
se.why: A sliding scale and patients paying nothing point to people with little money: indigent and impoverished. Affluent reverses the logic, and the remaining choices have no bearing on fees.

se.q: The prolonged drought threatened to _____ the reservoir entirely, and engineers began drawing up plans to pipe water from a neighboring watershed.
se.why: A drought that forces engineers to import water would use the reservoir up: deplete and exhaust. Replenish and augment are a synonym pair in the wrong direction, and contaminate is not what a drought does.

se.q: Though her family had been wealthy for generations, a series of disastrous investments left the heiress almost _____, forced to sell the ancestral estate to pay her creditors.
se.why: 'Though... wealthy' plus selling the estate to pay creditors indicates near-total poverty: destitute and penniless. Solvent and affluent describe the former wealth the sentence contrasts with.

title: Fleeting & Fickle
rule: This cluster combines brevity in time (ephemeral, evanescent, transient, transitory) with instability of mind or mood (capricious, mercurial, fickle, volatile, vacillate). The GRE tests these words through contrasts with permanence ('seemed to promise a lasting career,' 'loyal to no single movement'), and a common trap is confusing a short-lived thing with a changeable person: decide whether the sentence is about duration or about unpredictability.
tip: Ephemeral is Greek for 'lasting a day,' like the mayfly (order Ephemeroptera), while mercurial comes from Mercury, the swift, shifty messenger god and the restless liquid metal named for him.

words.m: lasting for a very short time
words.s: Fashion trends have always been ephemeral, but social media has shortened their life span from several seasons to a matter of weeks.

words.m: soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; vanishing
words.s: The painter sought to capture the evanescent glow of dusk, working rapidly before the light faded and the colors of the harbor turned gray.

words.m: lasting only a short time; temporary
words.s: The doctor assured him that the dizziness was transient, a common side effect that would disappear once his body adjusted to the medication.
words.root: Latin transire, 'to go across, pass by'

words.m: not permanent; existing only briefly
words.s: The economist cautioned that the surge in employment might prove transitory, driven by seasonal hiring rather than any lasting improvement in the economy.

words.m: changing loyalties, interests, or affections frequently
words.s: Pop stars learn quickly that their audience is fickle, abandoning yesterday's idol the moment a newer, younger face appears on the charts.

words.m: given to sudden, unaccountable changes of mood or behavior
words.s: Employees never knew what to expect from the capricious director, who might praise a proposal on Monday and ridicule the identical plan on Friday.
words.root: Italian capriccio, 'sudden start,' like a skittish goat (capra)

words.m: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
words.s: The conductor's mercurial temperament made rehearsals exhausting: he could pass from exuberant praise to icy fury in the span of a single measure.
words.root: From Mercury, swift god and shifting liquid metal

words.m: liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse
words.s: Investors fled the volatile market after a week in which share prices swung wildly, gaining and losing a fifth of their value within days.

words.m: to waver between different opinions or actions; to be indecisive
words.s: Voters grew impatient as the candidate continued to vacillate on the pipeline, endorsing it in oil country and opposing it on college campuses.
words.root: Latin vacillare, 'to sway to and fro'

words.m: frequently changing; not faithful or dependable
words.s: In the sonnet, the moon serves as an emblem of the inconstant lover, waxing and waning as her affections shift from one suitor to the next.

words.m: acting in a fanciful, unpredictable, impulsive way
words.s: The monarch's whimsical decrees, banning beards one month and mandating them the next, left his subjects anxious about what might be forbidden tomorrow.
words.root: From whim, a sudden fanciful notion

words.m: liable to change; changeable
words.s: Early astronomers held that the heavens were perfect and unchanging, while the earthly realm alone was mutable and subject to decay.

tc.q: Although the fame that followed his viral video seemed at first to promise a lasting career, it proved _____: within a year, few people could recall his name.
tc.why: 'Although... seemed... lasting' sets up a contrast, and 'within a year, few... could recall' confirms short-lived fame: ephemeral. Enduring is the expectation the sentence overturns.

tc.q: The board found it impossible to plan around the founder's _____ leadership; strategic priorities that he championed at one meeting were often abandoned without explanation at the next.
tc.why: Priorities championed at one meeting and abandoned without explanation at the next define capricious leadership. Autocratic is the trap: it describes control, not unpredictability.

tc.q: The dye's colors were brilliant but (i) _____, fading within weeks of exposure to sunlight; the medieval weavers who nonetheless preferred it seem to have valued immediate splendor over (ii) _____.
tc.why: The appositive defines the first blank: 'fading within weeks' means evanescent, and indelible is its opposite. Preferring 'immediate splendor' implies sacrificing lasting color: durability.

tc.q: Political scientists have long noted that public opinion on the issue is remarkably (i) _____: support for the policy has swung by more than twenty points several times in a single decade. Yet legislators, oddly, treat each new poll as though it revealed a (ii) _____ conviction.
tc.why: Repeated twenty-point swings mark opinion as volatile, the opposite of entrenched. 'Yet... oddly' means legislators treat each poll as reflecting a fixed view, a settled conviction, rather than a fleeting one.

se.q: Critics have described the poet's true subject as the _____ quality of happiness, which her verses present as a series of brief illuminations that vanish almost as soon as they are noticed.
se.why: 'Brief illuminations that vanish almost as soon as they are noticed' defines short-lived happiness: evanescent and transient. Enduring and abiding form a synonym pair pointing the wrong way.

se.q: Loyal to no single artistic movement, the critic was notoriously _____ in her enthusiasms, championing abstract expressionism one season and dismissing it as a passing fad the next.
se.why: Championing a movement one season and dismissing it the next shows changeable enthusiasm: fickle and inconstant. Steadfast is the opposite, and dogmatic would mean she never wavered.

se.q: Unable to decide whether to accept the overseas posting, he continued to _____ for weeks, telling friends one day that he would go and the next that he would stay.
se.why: Saying he would go one day and stay the next is the very definition of wavering between options: vacillate and waver. Persevere implies steady purpose, and acquiesce implies he had already given in.

se.q: The country's _____ political climate, in which governments have risen and fallen five times in a single decade, has made foreign investors reluctant to commit capital.
se.why: Five governments in a decade signals rapid, unpredictable change: volatile and unstable. Stable and placid pair up but contradict the turnover, and stagnant implies no change at all.

title: Permanent & Entrenched
rule: This cluster describes what lasts or cannot be dislodged: qualities that never change (immutable, perpetual, imperishable), that recur over long spans (perennial, chronic), or that are fixed deep by habit and time (inveterate, ingrained, entrenched, ossify). The GRE often sets these against reformers or new evidence ('despite decades of campaigns,' 'reformers had hoped'), and a common trap is reading perennial as merely 'yearly' or confusing an ingrained habit with a deliberate, stubborn choice.
tip: Inveterate holds Latin vetus, 'old' (as in veteran): grown old in a habit; ossify means 'to turn to bone' (os), the fate of an idea that stops living and goes rigid.

words.m: unchanging over time or unable to be changed
words.s: The physicist questioned whether the so-called constants of nature are truly immutable or might have drifted slightly since the early universe.

words.m: lasting a long time; recurring again and again
words.s: Funding shortfalls are a perennial complaint among public school teachers, voiced in nearly every budget cycle for the past half century.
words.root: Latin per, 'through' + annus, 'year': through the years

words.m: never ending or changing; occurring repeatedly without interruption
words.s: Living in perpetual fear of eviction, the tenants hesitated to report even dangerous violations such as broken heaters and exposed wiring.

words.m: unable to be removed or forgotten; permanent
words.s: The war left an indelible mark on the novelist, whose later books return obsessively to the bombed city of his childhood.

words.m: having a long-established habit or practice unlikely to change
words.s: An inveterate gambler, he promised his family he would stop after each ruinous loss, only to return to the tables within days.
words.root: Latin vetus, 'old': grown old in a habit

words.m: firmly fixed or established, so as to be difficult to change
words.s: Prejudices so ingrained are rarely dislodged by statistics alone; they usually yield only to sustained personal contact with the people once feared.
words.root: Dyed 'in grain': colored through the very fiber

words.m: firmly established and difficult or unlikely to change
words.s: Reformers underestimated how entrenched the patronage system had become, with nearly every municipal job tied to loyalty to the party machine.
words.root: Dug into a trench, hence hard to dislodge

words.m: lasting a long time; enduring
words.s: Her abiding love of the sea, first kindled during childhood summers on the coast, eventually led her to a career in marine biology.

words.m: to become rigid and unable to change; literally, to turn into bone
words.s: Without fresh members and outside criticism, even a once-radical movement can ossify into a rigid orthodoxy that its founders would not recognize.

words.m: unable to be destroyed or removed
words.s: The inquiry concluded that corruption was not ineradicable, as cynics claimed, but simply had never been confronted by officials willing to prosecute it.

words.m: enduring forever; not subject to decay
words.s: The pharaohs built in stone because they hoped to leave imperishable monuments, structures that would outlast not only their dynasties but time itself.

words.m: persisting for a long time or constantly recurring
words.s: The town's chronic flooding, which returns every spring despite repeated promises of a new levee, has driven many families to sell their homes.

tc.q: Although the revolution swept away the monarchy within months, the deference to rank that had flourished under it proved far more _____, surviving in the manners and speech of ordinary citizens for generations.
tc.why: 'Although... within months' contrasts the monarchy's quick fall with deference 'surviving... for generations': entrenched. Ephemeral and precarious describe the monarchy, not the lingering habits.

tc.q: The professor's insistence that the rules of grammar are _____ struck his students as odd, since he spent half of each lecture tracing how English usage had shifted over the centuries.
tc.why: The claim seems odd only because he documents how usage 'had shifted,' so he must have called grammar unchanging: immutable. Prescriptive is the trap; rules that prescribe usage are not contradicted by usage changing over time.

tc.q: Reformers had hoped the new curriculum would revitalize the academy, but within a decade it had (i) _____ into a set of rote exercises, defended by faculty whose (ii) _____ attachment to routine made any further change unthinkable.
tc.why: 'Hoped... revitalize, but' signals the opposite outcome: the curriculum hardened into rote exercises, so ossified. An attachment that makes change 'unthinkable' is long-standing and habitual: inveterate, not tentative.

tc.q: Though the scandal (i) _____ the senator's reputation for a time, it left no (ii) _____ stain: within a few years, voters remembered him chiefly for the bridge he had funded.
tc.why: 'Though... for a time' and voters' later memories show the damage did not last: the scandal tarnished his reputation but left no indelible stain. Burnished reverses the scandal's effect, and 'no fleeting stain' or 'no superficial stain' would make the colon's explanation illogical.

se.q: Despite decades of public-health campaigns, smoking remains _____ in certain communities, where the habit is passed from one generation to the next almost as a rite of passage.
se.why: 'Despite decades of... campaigns' and a habit handed down through generations signal something deeply fixed: ingrained and entrenched. Waning and dwindling are a synonym pair that contradict 'remains.'

se.q: The dispute over water rights is a _____ feature of politics in the arid West, flaring up in nearly every legislative session for more than a century.
se.why: 'Nearly every legislative session for more than a century' marks a long-recurring issue: perennial and recurrent. Sporadic is the trap; it means occasional and irregular, not nearly every session.

se.q: An _____ optimist, she greeted each failed experiment as valuable data rather than a setback, a habit of mind her colleagues found alternately inspiring and exasperating.
se.why: Greeting 'each' failure the same way describes a deeply habitual trait: inveterate and incorrigible (an 'incorrigible optimist' cannot be cured of it). Occasional contradicts 'each,' and erstwhile and ostensible undercut the present, genuine habit.

se.q: The tour guide insisted that the lovers' initials, carved into the cathedral's stone in the fourteenth century, were _____, though restorers privately admitted they could sand them away in an afternoon.
se.why: 'Though' contrasts the guide's claim with the restorers' admission that the carvings are easily removed, so the guide called them permanent: indelible and ineradicable. Faded and illegible pair up but create no contrast with 'sand them away.'
